newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-BMW off to quick start in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BMW off to quick start in 1997.

text.p: German luxury carmaker Bayerische Motoren Werke AG (BMW) has kept pace with last year's strong performance, announcing on Thursday that sales surged 17.4 percent in the first five months of this year.

Speaking at the company's annual shareholders' meeting, BMW chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder said that from January to May sales climbed to 24.3 billion marks ($14.4 billion) from 20.7 billion in the same period a year earlier.
BMW intentially took some of the lustre off the strong figures, repeating a warning that growth rates could slow in the second half of the year.
Pischetsrieder said sales accelerated strongly in the second half of last year, making it difficult to maintain sales growth this year on a comparable basis.
"We expect stable developments in the number of cars sold to continue for all of 1997, Pischetsrieder said in the text of a speech presented to shareholders.
Group deliveries increased at a more moderate rate than sales, but still showed respectable eight percent growth to 497,000 units.
Deliveries of BMWs climbed to 288,000 units from 260,700 while deliveries of cars made by BMW's British unit, Rover Group, climbed to 209,000 from 201,100 units.

The figures are the latest sign of BMW's improving financial performance. In 1996 net profit climbed to 820 million marks from 692 million marks while sales surged to 52.3 billion marks from 46.1 billion.
Demand for BMWs has been strong because of continued healthy buying of the now aging 3-Series model, the new executive class saloon, the 5-Series, and the popular Z3 roadster sportscar.
Rover cars, meanwhile, made deeper inroads overseas with new models and a revamped sales network. BMW, which bought Rover in 1994, has made improving Rover exports a top priority.
Pischetsrieder, who has been criticised in some quarters for buying money-losing Rover, repeated his belief that the car maker would be in the black by 2000.
Rover lost 67 million marks last year but a BMW spokesman said that loss would shrink this year.

Group exports reached a new high. Registations in western Europe outside Germany climbed four percent to 90,000 units and surged 28 percent in the United States to 50,000 units. Exports to Japan increased 32 percent to 16,000 units.
Elsewhere, company sources said BMW would consider converting the denomination of its shares to euros from marks when Europe adopted a single currency in 1999.
